description: Somos a Timeout Zero: uma equipe movida por paciência, método e curiosidade. Acreditamos que um problema difícil se resolve entendendo-o a fundo antes de propor qualquer solução. Nosso objetivo é transformar dados reais da NASA em respostas claras e úteis, com foco em lacunas que ainda não foram resolvidas. Buscamos 2-3 pessoas que gostem de investigar, questionar e construir juntas: perfis de análise de dados, geoespacial, visualização e comunicação de ideias. Aqui ninguém desiste por tempo.
summary: Régua de Fogo (Fire Ruler) is a web app that turns more than 20 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning activity calendar. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) can't be compared directly: VIIRS sees smaller fires and counts about 6 times more hotspots, so joining the raw records draws a false jump in 2012. We convert the MODIS record to the VIIRS scale with one ratio per calendar month, learned from the years both sensors flew together. On years the method never saw, the monthly error is 7.2%, and the harmonized series matches Brazil's independent INPE reference with a 0.985 correlation (-0.13 without harmonization). The same scripts beat a single ratio in 9 of 11 regions tested worldwide. The app covers Bahia, Brazil, from 2003 to October 2026: a fire calendar, the current month against the historical normal, any area drawn on the map, hotspots of any day on the map, CSV download, and a full methodology and tests window. Fire brigades and land managers get a long, consistent history to plan the critical season, instead of a sensor artifact.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Fire brigades, emergency teams, land managers and scientists can see, for Bahia or any area inside it, which months and years burned the most since 2003, whether the current month is above or below the historical normal, and how one month compares across all years. Every view can be filtered by area and period and downloaded as CSV. The app is in English, with a Portuguese version at https://regua-queimadas.vercel.app/pt/

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: we processed 39.4 million NASA FIRMS hotspot records for Brazil (2003 to 2025), from MODIS Collection 6.1 (Aqua and Terra) and VIIRS 375 m (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20). After filters (vegetation fires only, low confidence removed), 3.6 million fall in Bahia. 2026 comes from the FIRMS area API. A sample check against the FIRMS API matched VIIRS exactly in 28 of 28 windows and MODIS within 0.15%.

2. Harmonization: for each calendar month, the ratio between VIIRS and MODIS Aqua hotspots in the years both flew (Aqua passes in the afternoon, close to VIIRS). In the rainy season fires are small and VIIRS sees many more of them, so the ratio goes from 5.7 in the dry season to 9.6 in January. From 2012 on, the series uses real VIIRS counts.

3. Validation: calibrated on 2012 to 2019 and tested on 2020 to 2023, a 7.2% monthly error with +0.2% bias; leaving one year out at a time (2013 to 2023) gave 7.1%. Seven methods were compared on the same test: single ratio, monthly ratio, grid cell-days, quantile mapping, a weighted factor model with NASA POWER weather data, a Terra-based ratio and a blend. The simplest robust one won. External check against INPE's reference satellite series: correlation 0.985, same peak month in 21 of 23 years, and the 2012 jump disappears.

4. Uncertainty: before 2012 the two MODIS satellites disagree, so the app shows a band between the Aqua, Terra and factor-model readings instead of a single number. Days with satellite outages are flagged.

5. Replication: the same scripts, run on FIRMS country files for Argentina, Australia, Bolivia, Canada, Chile, Indonesia, Mexico, Portugal, South Africa and the United States, beat a single ratio in 9 of 11 regions. Canada and Portugal show the limits: very seasonal or small fire regimes need more care.

6. Web app: static HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Apache ECharts, Leaflet, OpenStreetMap), with two small serverless functions on Vercel that read FIRMS server-side, so the API key never reaches the browser.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

A consistent record shows the real trend instead of an artifact of the satellite change, so fire managers can plan the critical season with history that is comparable year to year. Ground records show why satellites matter: for every fire registered by federal brigades in Bahia (IBAMA), the satellites saw about 2,085 hotspots.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of a black box, a ruler: 12 monthly numbers anyone can check in a spreadsheet, tested against 6 alternatives and against independent agencies, with an honest uncertainty band where the data disagree. Every number in the app comes from a script that can be rerun.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Color ramps readable for color blindness, English and Portuguese, mobile layout, provisional recent months marked as such, satellite outages and degraded MODIS days flagged, and the FIRMS key kept on the server.

TOOLS

Python (numpy) for data processing and validation; JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the app; Apache ECharts; Leaflet; OpenStreetMap; Vercel; GitHub.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

The full app covers Bahia; the method was replicated in 10 other countries with the same scripts. August to October 2026 are provisional near real time data. Next: a neural network for small areas and short-term fire forecasting, weather context per year, alerts for brigades and more regions.

SOURCE CODE

https://github.com/RafaTheMonk/calendario-queimadas
